title: Lowering the Voting Age to 16
resolution: Resolved: The voting age in the United States should be lowered to 16.
summary: A few U.S. cities and several countries let 16-year-olds vote. Should the whole country?

background.p: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971 in about three months, lowered the voting age in all U.S. elections from 21 to 18. Changing it for federal elections again would take another constitutional amendment, but cities can set rules for their own local elections. About a dozen cities in California, Maryland, New Jersey and Vermont let 16- and 17-year-olds vote in some local elections; Takoma Park, Maryland, was the first. Austria lowered its voting age to 16 in 2007, and the United Kingdom decided in July 2025 to lower it to 16 nationwide.

Supporters cite studies finding that 16-year-olds score similarly to adults on civic knowledge and skills, that youth turnout in Takoma Park was about double that of older voters, and that voting early can build a lifelong habit. Opponents point to the law's other age limits, low civics scores on national tests, and polls showing most Americans oppose the change.

positions: Studies such as Hart and Atkins (2011) find 16-year-olds similar to adults on civic knowledge and skills, and an Austrian study found their vote choices of similar quality.
Others point to brain development in the teen years and to national civics test scores as reasons for caution.

terms.def: The 1971 amendment that set the voting age at 18 for all U.S. elections.
The idea that people who vote in their first eligible election are more likely to keep voting.
An election for city, county or school board offices, which cities can sometimes open to younger voters.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Sixteen-year-olds are ready to vote, and starting earlier builds lifelong voters.

args.warrant: The skills voting requires (gathering information and weighing options calmly) are in place by 16, unlike quick decisions under pressure.
args.evidence: Hart and Atkins (2011) on civic knowledge and skills; Wagner and colleagues on vote quality in Austria.
args.response: The negative answers that national civics test scores are low, and many young voters may copy their parents.

args.claim: Voting at 16 builds a lifelong habit.
args.warrant: At 16, most young people live at home and attend school, where teachers and families can help them vote for the first time; at 18, many are moving and miss their first election.
args.evidence: Takoma Park turnout among 16- and 17-year-olds (about double that of older voters); research on habit formation in voting.
args.response: The negative replies that Takoma Park is a small, unusual city, and results there may not carry over.

args.claim: Young people have a stake in decisions.
args.warrant: Sixteen-year-olds work, pay taxes, drive and live with the long-term results of today's choices on schools, debt and the environment.
args.evidence: Labor data on teen employment and taxes; examples of policies with long-term effects.
args.response: The negative argues that many rights and duties begin at 18, and voting fits with them.

args.claim: Other democracies have done it without harm.
args.warrant: When countries like Austria lowered the voting age, they didn't see worse elections, suggesting the fears are overstated.
args.evidence: Austria (2007) and the UK's 2025 decision; studies of Austrian young voters.
args.response: The negative replies that a few countries' experience is limited, and U.S. civic education differs.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Eighteen is the right line: it matches adulthood in law and gives time for civic learning.

args.claim: The law treats 18 as adulthood for good reasons.
args.warrant: We don't let 16-year-olds sign contracts, serve on juries or enlist without permission; voting, which decides laws for everyone, belongs with those adult responsibilities.
args.evidence: Ages set in federal and state law; Britannica's summary of the opposing case.
args.response: The affirmative answers that many ages already differ (driving at 16, drinking at 21), so there's no single age of adulthood.

args.claim: Many teens haven't finished their civic education.
args.warrant: Students often take government classes late in high school; letting them vote first puts the ballot ahead of the lesson.
args.evidence: NAEP civics results (2022: 20% of eighth-graders proficient); state civics course requirements.
args.response: The affirmative replies that many adults also score poorly on civics tests, and we don't test adults before voting.

args.claim: Teens may be more influenced by parents and teachers.
args.warrant: Most 16-year-olds live at home and spend their days at school, so their votes may echo the adults around them rather than independent judgment.
args.evidence: Research on political socialization in families; Britannica's summary of the opposing case.
args.response: The affirmative answers that adults are also influenced by family and friends, and teens often disagree with their parents.

args.warrant: Changing who votes is a basic change to democracy and should have broad agreement, which this lacks.
args.evidence: Polls showing large majorities opposed, such as a 2019 Hill-HarrisX poll (84% opposed).
args.response: The affirmative replies that lowering the age to 18 was once unpopular too, and rights shouldn't depend on polls.

strawmen.why: The proposal concerns 16- and 17-year-olds, not young children.
strawmen.steelman: Sixteen-year-olds have the civic skills to vote, and starting while they're at home and in school builds lifelong voting habits, as Takoma Park and Austria suggest.

strawmen.why: Opponents argue about legal adulthood, civic education and independence, not intelligence.
strawmen.steelman: Eighteen matches the other responsibilities of adulthood, gives time for civic education, and the change lacks broad public support.

weak.arg: If you can drive, you can vote.
weak.why: Driving and voting require different things; this analogy is easy to attack.
A slippery slope with no evidence of the later steps.

aff: How would the change happen for federal elections?
How big is Takoma Park, and how many young people voted?
neg: What did studies find about 16-year-olds' civic knowledge compared with adults?
Do we test adults' civics knowledge before they vote?
